```{r linear-mixed-models-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
library(car)
library(DHARMa)
library(effectsize)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(emmeans)
library(performance)
library(patchwork)
library(janitor)
library(tidyverse)

options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))
options(scipen = 999)  # no sci notation

u_df <- read_csv("data/andrew.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  # Map to Quinn & Keough's Table 9.1 densities. NOTE the file's dens_33 /
  # dens_66 labels are the reverse of the book's percentages -- verified by
  # matching patch means: dens_33 is the book's 66% group, dens_66 its 33%.
  mutate(treat = case_when(
           treat == "removal" ~ "0%",     # book   0% density, mean algae 39.2
           treat == "dens_66" ~ "33%",    # book  33% density, mean algae 19.0
           treat == "dens_33" ~ "66%",    # book  66% density, mean algae 21.6
           treat == "control" ~ "100%"),  # book 100% density, mean algae  1.3
         treat = factor(treat, levels = c("0%", "33%", "66%", "100%")),
         patch = as_factor(patch))

u_summary <- u_df %>%
  group_by(treat) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(algae), sd = sd(algae),
            se = sd / sqrt(n), min = min(algae), max = max(algae))
```

- Poisson and negative binomial for counts; overdispersion
- Logistic regression and the odds ratio

And from the ANOVA weeks — **factorial designs**:

- Two crossed factors, main effects and an interaction

Today the second factor is **not** crossed with the first, and we do not

Last week changed the **distribution** of the response. This week

## Part 1 · The Data, and Why a One-Way ANOVA Fails It {.divider}

## Data Overview {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
`treat` — urchin density treatment (0 / 33 / 66 / 100%)
`patch` — **four patches nested inside each treatment, 16 in all**
`quad` — 5 replicate quadrats within every patch
`algae` — % cover of filamentous algae, the response

```{r linear-mixed-models-02}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
head(u_df, 4)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-03}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
u_summary %>%
  dplyr::select(treat, n, mean, sd) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

::: callout-note
**📖 The gradient is not monotonic**

39.2 → 19.0 → 21.6 → 1.3. The 33% and 66% means sit within noise of
each other. That is the data, not an error — and it is part of why the
treatment effect comes out non-significant.
:::
:::
:::::

## The Design Is Hierarchical, Not Factorial {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
`treat` and `patch` are **not crossed**. Patch 7 exists only inside one
treatment; there is no "patch 7 of the 0% treatment *and* of the 100%
treatment."

That is a **nested**, or hierarchical, design:

$$\text{treatment} \rightarrow \text{patch} \rightarrow \text{quadrat}$$

The 5 quadrats in a patch are **subsamples of that patch**, not 5
independent replicates of the treatment. The treatment was applied to
the **patch**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**⚠️ So what is *n*?**

For testing `treat` there are **16** experimental units, not 80. Four
patches per treatment.

Treating the 80 quadrats as independent replicates of the treatment is
**pseudoreplication** (Hurlbert 1984) — the single most common fatal
flaw in ecological statistics.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 The giveaway question**

*"What did I apply the treatment to?"* Count those. If you measured
more things than you manipulated, the extra measurements are
subsamples.
:::
:::
:::::

## Three Levels in One Picture

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r lmm-levels-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-alt: "Algae cover plotted for each of the sixteen patches, grouped into four panels by urchin density. Grey dots are the eighty quadrats, blue diamonds are the sixteen patch means, and an orange horizontal line in each panel is the treatment mean. Patch means scatter widely around their treatment line."
lv_patch <- u_df %>%
  group_by(treat, patch) %>%
  summarise(patch_mean = mean(algae), .groups = "drop")

lv_treat <- lv_patch %>%
  group_by(treat) %>%
  summarise(treat_mean = mean(patch_mean), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(u_df, aes(patch, algae)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey55", alpha = 0.7, size = 1.2,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  geom_point(data = lv_patch, aes(y = patch_mean),
             colour = "#0072B2", size = 3, shape = 18) +
  geom_hline(data = lv_treat, aes(yintercept = treat_mean),
             colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_grid(. ~ treat, scales = "free_x", switch = "x") +
  labs(x = "Patch, grouped by urchin density", y = "Algae cover (%)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
Every quadrat's algae cover is three things added together:

1. its **treatment mean** — the [orange line]{style="color:#D55E00"}
2. how far its **patch** sits from that line — orange to
   [blue diamond]{style="color:#0072B2"}
3. how far the **quadrat** sits from its patch — diamond to grey dot

::: callout-important
**That sentence is the whole model**

Everything today is about pieces 2 and 3: **how big each kind of
scatter is**, and which one the treatment has to beat.

The treatment was applied to patches, so it has to beat piece 2.
:::
:::
:::::

## Pseudoreplication, Priced {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Same 80 numbers, two models. The only difference is what the treatment
is tested against:

```{r lmm-pseudo-01}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
a_ps <- summary(aov(algae ~ treat + treat:patch,
                    data = u_df))[[1]]

round(a_ps[, c("Df", "Sum Sq", "Mean Sq")], 1)

c(naive_F  = a_ps[1, "Mean Sq"] / a_ps[3, "Mean Sq"],
  nested_F = a_ps[1, "Mean Sq"] / a_ps[2, "Mean Sq"]
  ) %>% round(2)
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**16.11 against 2.72**

Both divide $MS_{treat}$ = 4810. The **naive** model divides by
$MS_{resid}$ = 298.6, the quadrat-to-quadrat noise. The **correct** one
divides by $MS_{patch(treat)}$ = 1770.2, the patch-to-patch noise.

*p* goes from **0.00000007** to **0.091** — from a headline result to
nothing — on exactly the same data.
:::

The traditional fix is to name the error stratum by hand:

``` r
aov(algae ~ treat + Error(patch), data = u_df)
```

**That is what the rest of this lecture replaces.**
:::
:::::

## What If Urchins Did Nothing at All?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r lmm-sim-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-alt: "Two histograms of p-values from one thousand simulated experiments with no treatment effect. Ignoring patch, the leftmost bar below 0.05 holds about half of all experiments. With the mixed model the histogram is flat and the bar below 0.05 holds about five percent."
set.seed(2026)
sim_reef <- function() {
  d <- expand_grid(treat = factor(1:4), p = 1:4, q = 1:5) %>%
    mutate(patch = interaction(treat, p))
  d$y <- 30 + rnorm(16, 0, 17)[as.integer(d$patch)] + rnorm(80, 0, 17)
  c(naive = anova(lm(y ~ treat, data = d))[1, "Pr(>F)"],
    mixed = suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(
      anova(lmer(y ~ treat + (1 | patch), data = d))[1, "Pr(>F)"])))
}
sim_p  <- as_tibble(t(replicate(1000, sim_reef())))
sim_fp <- round(100 * colMeans(sim_p < 0.05))

sim_p %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "model", values_to = "p") %>%
  mutate(model = if_else(
    model == "naive",
    paste0("Ignore patch: ", sim_fp["naive"], "% false alarms"),
    paste0("Mixed model: ", sim_fp["mixed"], "% false alarms"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(fill = p < 0.05), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05),
                 colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey70", "#D55E00"), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = "p-value for treatment", y = "Simulated experiments") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
1000 made-up reefs, laid out like the real one — 4 treatments, 4
patches each, 5 quadrats each, and the same patch and quadrat scatter
as the real data. **The treatment does nothing in any of them.**

A fair test cries wolf 5% of the time.

::: callout-important
**Ignoring patch cries wolf about half the time**

With no effect at all, four treatment means still differ — each is an
average of only **4 patches**, and patches differ a lot. Judge that
against quadrat noise and it looks far too big to be chance.
:::

The mixed model in the right panel is what Parts 2–6 build.
:::
:::::

## Where the Variation Goes

::::: columns
::: {.column width="42%"}
One quadrat's distance from the grand mean splits into **three** pieces,
not two:

$$\underbrace{(Y_{ijk} - \bar{Y})}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{(\bar{Y}_i - \bar{Y})}_{A} + \underbrace{(\bar{Y}_{ij} - \bar{Y}_i)}_{B(A)} + \underbrace{(Y_{ijk} - \bar{Y}_{ij})}_{\text{resid}}$$

Square and sum over all 80 quadrats:

$$SS_{total} = SS_A + SS_{B(A)} + SS_{resid}$$

On these data: **54 781 = 14 429 + 21 242 + 19 110**.

::: callout-note
**The middle row is the whole point**

A one-way ANOVA has no $SS_{B(A)}$ row — that variation lands in the
residual. Here it is **bigger than the treatment effect**, and it is
what the treatment must be tested against.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r lmm-pseudo-02}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-alt: "Four stacked panels showing the nested sums-of-squares allocation on the sea urchin data. Panel one, SS total: every quadrat's deviation from the dashed grand-mean line. Panel two, SS_A: each of the four treatment means' deviation from the grand mean. Panel three, SS_B(A): each of the sixteen patch means' deviation from its own treatment mean. Panel four, SS residual: every quadrat's deviation from its own patch mean."
ss_df <- u_df %>%
  arrange(treat, patch) %>%
  mutate(patch = fct_inorder(patch)) %>%
  group_by(treat) %>% mutate(treat_mean = mean(algae)) %>%
  group_by(treat, patch) %>% mutate(patch_mean = mean(algae)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(grand = mean(algae), x = as.numeric(patch))

pm <- ss_df %>% distinct(treat, patch, x, patch_mean, treat_mean, grand)

tm <- ss_df %>%
  group_by(treat) %>%
  summarise(x = mean(x), xmin = min(x) - 0.45, xmax = max(x) + 0.45,
            treat_mean = first(treat_mean), grand = first(grand),
            .groups = "drop")

set.seed(42)
pts <- ss_df %>% mutate(xj = x + runif(n(), -0.22, 0.22))

base <- function(p, ttl) {
  p +
    scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = tm$x, labels = levels(ss_df$treat)) +
    labs(title = ttl, x = NULL, y = "Algae (%)") +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-5, 82)) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 9, face = "bold"),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}

p1 <- base(
  ggplot(pts) +
    geom_segment(aes(xj, xend = xj, y = grand, yend = algae, colour = treat),
                 alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_point(aes(xj, algae, colour = treat), size = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = ss_df$grand[1], linetype = "dashed"),
  expression(SS[total] * ": every quadrat vs. grand mean"))

p2 <- base(
  ggplot(tm) +
    geom_segment(aes(x, xend = x, y = grand, yend = treat_mean, colour = treat),
                 linewidth = 1.1) +
    geom_segment(aes(xmin, xend = xmax, y = treat_mean, yend = treat_mean,
                     colour = treat), linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = ss_df$grand[1], linetype = "dashed"),
  expression(SS[A] * ": treatment means vs. grand mean"))

p3 <- base(
  ggplot(pm) +
    geom_segment(aes(x, xend = x, y = treat_mean, yend = patch_mean,
                     colour = treat), linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(aes(x, patch_mean, colour = treat), size = 1.4) +
    geom_segment(data = tm, aes(xmin, xend = xmax, y = treat_mean,
                                yend = treat_mean),
                 linewidth = 0.5, colour = "grey30"),
  expression(SS[B(A)] * ": patch means vs. their treatment mean"))

p4 <- base(
  ggplot(pts) +
    geom_segment(aes(xj, xend = xj, y = patch_mean, yend = algae,
                     colour = treat), alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_point(aes(xj, algae, colour = treat), size = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_segment(data = pm, aes(x = x - 0.35, xend = x + 0.35, y = patch_mean,
                                yend = patch_mean),
                 linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey30"),
  expression(SS[residual] * ": quadrats vs. their own patch mean"))

p1 / p2 / p3 / p4
```
:::
:::::

## Pseudoreplication Corrupts the *p*-Value, Not the Effect Size {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r lmm-pseudo-03}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
e_nested <- eta_squared(
  aov(algae ~ treat + Error(patch), data = u_df))$Eta2_partial
e_naive <- eta_squared(
  aov(algae ~ treat + patch, data = u_df))$Eta2_partial[1]

data.frame(
  model = c("Nested (correct)", "Naive (pseudoreplicated)"),
  partial_eta2 = round(c(e_nested, e_naive), 2),
  p = c("0.091", "0.00000007"))
```

The wrong model and the right model agree the treatment effect is
**large** — 0.40 against 0.43.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**What they disagree about is confidence**

Seven orders of magnitude in *p*, and almost nothing in effect size.
Pseudoreplication does not invent an effect. It invents **certainty**.
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 So what is the honest conclusion?**

Not "urchins do not affect algae." It is **"a large effect that four
patches per treatment could not resolve"** — a power problem, and the
effect size is what lets you say so.

Hold onto that. In Part 5 the variance components will tell you
*exactly why* four patches were not enough, and what to do about it.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 2 · Fixed, Random, and the Mixed Model {.divider}

## What Makes an Effect "Random"?

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
Ask one question: **do I care about these specific levels, or are they a
sample of levels I could have had?**

::: {.compact-table}
| | `treat` | `patch` |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| The levels are | 0/33/66/100% density | patches 1–16 |
| Chosen by | me, deliberately | whatever was there |
| Would a repeat study use the same ones? | **yes** | no — different patches |
| I want to estimate | **each level's mean** | **how much they vary** |
| So it is | **fixed** | **random** |
:::

::: callout-important
**The key consequence**

A fixed factor with 16 levels costs you **15 parameters**. A random
factor with 16 levels costs you **one** — a single variance,
σ²~patch~.

That is why mixed models cope with designs `aov()` chokes on: they are
estimating far less.
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 A useful test**

If you can write a sentence a reader would care about that names a
specific level — *"the 100% density treatment reduced algae"* — it is
**fixed**.

If the sentence would be *"patch 7 happened to be lush"* — nobody cares
about patch 7 in particular. **Random.**
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ You need enough levels**

Estimating a variance from **fewer than ~5 levels** is unreliable. With
2 or 3 groups, fit them as fixed effects instead.

We have 16 patches — comfortably enough. Parts 7 and 8 use **3 lakes**
and **3 streams**, and show what that costs.
:::
::::
:::::::

## Reading the Random-Effects Formula

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Read every random term as

$$(\ \text{what varies}\ \mid\ \text{across what}\ )$$

- **`(1|patch)`** — the `1` means the **intercept**. Each patch gets its
  own baseline algae cover.
- **`(1|treat:patch)`** — the same thing, just naming the group as the
  treatment-patch combination. Still intercept-only.
- **`(1 + range|lake)`** — *this* is a random **slope**: each lake gets
  its own intercept **and** its own `range` effect. Part 7 fits it on
  the crayfish, where it turns out to be the interaction in disguise.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ `(1|treat:patch)` is not a random slope**

Anything of the form `(1|...)` is **random intercepts only** — the `1`
*is* the intercept. What changes between `(1|patch)` and
`(1|treat:patch)` is the **grouping variable**, not what varies within
it.

Here they are the identical model, because patch IDs are already unique
(1–16) and each patch sits in one treatment. We will use `(1|patch)`.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 The rule**

You only have a random slope when something **other than `1`** appears
on the left of the `|`.
:::
:::
:::::

## Fitting It {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-05}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
u_lmer_model <- lmer(
  algae ~ treat + (1 | patch),
  data = u_df,
  control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

VarCorr(u_lmer_model)

fixef(u_lmer_model)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
The model in words:

$$algae_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + b_{j(i)} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$

- $\mu$ — the overall mean
- $\alpha_i$ — the **fixed** effect of treatment *i*
- $b_{j(i)}$ — the **random** effect of patch *j* in treatment *i*,
  $b \sim N(0,\ \sigma^2_{patch})$
- $\epsilon_{ijk}$ — the residual for quadrat *k*,
  $\epsilon \sim N(0,\ \sigma^2_{within})$

::: callout-important
Notice what the model estimates for `patch`: **not 16 numbers, one
number** — the variance those 16 patches were drawn from.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 3 · Testing the Fixed Effect {.divider}

## Two Tests, Two Answers {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-06}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
Anova(u_lmer_model, type = 3,
      test.statistic = "F")
```

```{r linear-mixed-models-07}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
Anova(u_lmer_model, type = 3,
      test.statistic = "Chisq")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**The *F*-test** (Kenward-Roger denominator df)

- Accounts for the uncertainty in the estimated variance components
- More conservative, better at small *n*
- Here: *F*~3,12~ = 2.72, ***p* = 0.091**

**The Wald χ²**

- Assumes the variance components are **known**, not estimated
- Assumes **infinite** denominator df, i.e. a large sample
- Here: χ²~3~ = 8.15, ***p* = 0.043**

χ² = *F* × numerator df = 2.717 × 3 = 8.15 — exactly. The only thing
that differs is the **reference distribution**: χ²~3~ assumes infinite
denominator df; *F*~3,12~ admits there are 12.
:::
:::::

## Same Model, Same Data, Opposite Conclusions

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.compact-table}
| Test | Statistic | *p* | Verdict at α = 0.05 |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| *F*, Kenward-Roger df | *F*~3,12~ = 2.72 | **0.091** | not significant |
| *F*, Satterthwaite df | *F*~3,12~ = 2.72 | **0.091** | not significant |
| Wald χ² | χ²~3~ = 8.15 | **0.043** | significant |
:::

**Rule of thumb: default to the *F*-test.** As the number of groups
grows its denominator df grow with them, and it converges on the χ² — so
you give up nothing by always using it, and you are protected when the
sample is small. The χ² is a **large-sample shortcut**, not a better
test.

We have **80 observations and 16 patches** — nowhere near large sample.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**⚠️ Report the *F*-test — and say which df you used**

The χ² is being over-confident. It pretends it knows σ²~patch~ and
σ²~within~ exactly, when they were estimated from 16 patches.

The *F*-test agrees with Part 1's `aov(Error(patch))` to four decimal
places, **because it is the same test**.
:::

::: callout-warning
**🖐 The uncomfortable part**

Run only the χ² and you report a significant effect and never know.
When two defensible analyses straddle α = 0.05, say so and justify the
choice — do not pick one and delete the other.
:::
:::
:::::

## Why `lme4` Prints No *p*-Values {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r lmm-pval-01}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
# the same model, fitted by lme4 alone
u_plain <- lme4::lmer(algae ~ treat + (1 | patch),
                      data = u_df)
round(coef(summary(u_plain)), 2)

# and by lmerTest (what library(lmerTest) gives you)
round(coef(summary(u_lmer_model)), 3)
```

Same estimates, same standard errors, same *t*. `lmerTest` adds two
columns: **df** and ***p***.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
The missing columns are deliberate. Douglas Bates, who wrote `lme4`,
left them out because:

- in `lm()` the denominator df is a simple count, and *t* and *F* follow
  their distributions **exactly**
- in a mixed model the denominator is built from **several estimated
  variances** — so the ratio is only approximately *F*, and there is
  **no single correct df**
- only balanced classical designs (like this one) give an exact answer

::: callout-note
**📖 What `lmerTest` does**

It fits the **identical model**, then approximates the df
(Satterthwaite by default, Kenward-Roger on request). The *p*-value is
a well-tested approximation, not an exact result — which is why you
report **which df method** you used.
:::
:::
:::::

## Four Routes to a *p*-Value

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r lmm-pval-02}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
pv_m1 <- lme4::lmer(algae ~ treat + (1 | patch), data = u_df, REML = FALSE)
pv_m0 <- lme4::lmer(algae ~ 1 + (1 | patch), data = u_df, REML = FALSE)
pv_pb <- pbkrtest::PBmodcomp(pv_m1, pv_m0, nsim = 1000, seed = 2026)

data.frame(
  method = c("Wald chi-square", "Likelihood-ratio test",
             "F, Kenward-Roger df", "Parametric bootstrap"),
  assumes = c("variances known exactly", "many groups",
              "df approximated", "nothing about df"),
  p = round(c(
    Anova(u_lmer_model, type = 3, test.statistic = "Chisq")["treat", "Pr(>Chisq)"],
    pv_pb$test["LRT", "p.value"],
    Anova(u_lmer_model, type = 3, test.statistic = "F")["treat", "Pr(>F)"],
    pv_pb$test["PBtest", "p.value"]), 3))
```

Ben Bolker (who maintains `lme4`) does not say "never use *p*-values".
He **ranks** the ways of getting one, crudest first — the order of this
table.

The **parametric bootstrap** simulates 1000 data sets from the model
with no treatment effect and asks how often the test statistic comes
out as large as ours. It assumes nothing about df.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**The two careful methods agree. The two shortcuts agree.**

The bootstrap, which makes no df assumption at all, lands on the
*F*-test — and on Part 1's `aov(Error(patch))`. The χ² and the
likelihood-ratio test both say "significant", and both are wrong for
the same reason: they behave as if 16 patches were many.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 For ecological data**

Groups are nearly always few. Use the ***F*-test with Kenward-Roger or
Satterthwaite df**. Reach for the bootstrap
(`pbkrtest::PBmodcomp()`) when a result sits near 0.05 and matters.

Better still, report the **estimate and its confidence interval**.
:::
:::
:::::

## Do I Still Need `contr.sum`?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
The first chunk of every lecture sets
`options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))`. What does that
change in a mixed model?

::: {.compact-table}
| Output | Changes with the contrast? |
|------------------------------|------------------|
| fitted values, variance components | **no** — same model |
| `emmeans()` and pairwise tests | **no** |
| `anova()` from `lmerTest` | **no** |
| `car::Anova(type = 3)`, model has an **interaction** | **yes** |
| what each row of `summary()` means | **yes** |
:::

It is **interactions**, not unbalanced data, that make the contrast
matter. With one factor, as here, every test is identical either way.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Why `car::Anova(type = 3)` cares**

It tests "is this coefficient zero". Under R's default treatment
contrasts, a main-effect coefficient is the effect **at the reference
level of the other factor** — not averaged across its levels.

Under `contr.sum` it is the **average** effect, which is what "main
effect" means.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 The habit**

Keep the `options(contrasts = ...)` line at the top of every script.
It is required for `car::Anova(type = 3)` with interactions and
harmless everywhere else. And read effects from **`emmeans()`**, never
from the rows of `summary()`.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 4 · How the Variance Actually Gets Estimated {.divider}

## The Question This Part Answers

For three weeks, **every** answer came from one move: take the total
sum of squares, cut it into pieces by source, divide each piece by its
df to get a mean square, and form a ratio.

$$SS_{total} = SS_{treat} + SS_{patch(treat)} + SS_{within}$$

`lmer()` printed σ²~patch~ = 294.3 and never showed you a sum of
squares anywhere.

::: callout-important
**So where did that number come from, and why is it not an SS table?**

The rest of this part is the answer. It is the single biggest
conceptual change between Part 1 and the rest of today — bigger than
the notation, bigger than the *p*-value.
:::

## The Old Route — Sums of Squares and Expected Mean Squares {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Part 1's table, one more time:

```{r lmm-ems-01}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
a_tab <- summary(aov(algae ~ treat + treat:patch,
                     data = u_df))[[1]]
round(a_tab[, c("Df", "Sum Sq", "Mean Sq")], 1)
```

Statistical theory tells you what each mean square estimates **on
average** — its *expected* mean square:

$$E[MS_{within}] = \sigma^2_{within}$$
$$E[MS_{patch}] = \sigma^2_{within} + n\,\sigma^2_{patch}$$
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
Now **set the observed equal to the expected and solve.** That is all
the old method is — two equations, two unknowns, no statistics at all
past this point:

$$\hat\sigma^2_{within} = MS_{within}$$
$$\hat\sigma^2_{patch} = \frac{MS_{patch} - MS_{within}}{n}$$

```{r lmm-ems-02}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
MS_patch  <- a_tab[2, "Mean Sq"]
MS_within <- a_tab[3, "Mean Sq"]
n <- 5                      # quadrats per patch

c(within = MS_within,
  patch  = (MS_patch - MS_within) / n)
```

This is the **method of moments**. It is arithmetic on a table.
:::
:::::

## The New Route — Write Down the Variance and Search for It

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
A mixed model never builds that table. It writes the variance of the
**whole response vector** in one matrix:

$$\mathbf{V} = \sigma^2_{patch}\,\mathbf{ZZ}^\top + \sigma^2_{within}\,\mathbf{I}$$

- $\mathbf{Z}$ says which patch each quadrat belongs to
- $\mathbf{ZZ}^\top$ is 1 for any two quadrats **in the same patch**,
  0 otherwise
- So $\mathbf{V}$ states, directly, that two quadrats in a patch are
  correlated and two in different patches are not

Then it asks a completely different question:

> **Which pair of numbers (σ²~patch~, σ²~within~) makes the data I
> actually observed most likely?**
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**That is the whole switch.**

**Old:** partition a quantity you computed (SS), then solve an algebraic
identity for the variances.

**New:** propose a pair of variances, ask how probable the data are
under them, and keep searching until that probability stops improving.

No decomposition. No table. **A search over a likelihood surface.**
:::

The *F*-ratio idea does not disappear — it comes back at the end, when
you test the fixed effect. But it is no longer how the variances are
obtained.
:::
:::::

## The Restricted Likelihood, Written Out {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
Eight lines, no `lme4`. This is literally what the optimizer is doing:

```{r lmm-reml-01}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
y <- u_df$algae
X <- model.matrix(~ treat, u_df)   # fixed effects
Z <- model.matrix(~ 0 + patch, u_df)   # grouping
ZZt <- Z %*% t(Z)

reml_ll <- function(v_patch, v_within) {
  V  <- v_patch * ZZt + v_within * diag(nrow(X))
  Vi <- solve(V)
  A  <- t(X) %*% Vi %*% X
  b  <- solve(A, t(X) %*% Vi %*% y)     # GLS fixed effects
  r  <- y - X %*% b
  -0.5 * as.numeric(determinant(V, log = TRUE)$modulus +
                    determinant(A, log = TRUE)$modulus +
                    t(r) %*% Vi %*% r)
}
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
Three pieces, each doing one job:

- $\log|\mathbf{V}|$ — penalises making the variances big, since a
  bigger variance spreads probability thinner
- $\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}$ — penalises leaving big
  residuals, which pushes the variances **up**
- $\log|\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}|$ — the
  **restricted** part, the correction for having estimated the fixed
  effects

The answer is the pair where those forces balance.

(An additive constant, $-\tfrac12 (n-p)\log 2\pi$, is left out — it
shifts the curve but not where the maximum is.)
:::
:::::

## The Surface the Optimizer Climbs

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r lmm-reml-02}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-alt: "Curve of the restricted log-likelihood against sigma-squared patch, rising steeply from a low value at zero, peaking near 294, and then declining very gradually. A dashed vertical line marks the maximum."

prof <- tibble(v = seq(0, 1200, length.out = 180)) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(ll = reml_ll(v, 298.6)) %>%
  ungroup()

best <- prof$v[which.max(prof$ll)]

ggplot(prof, aes(v, ll)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 294.31, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  annotate("text", x = 294.31, y = min(prof$ll), hjust = -0.08,
           label = "REML peak\n294.3", size = 2.9, color = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = expression(sigma[patch]^2),
       y = "Restricted log-likelihood") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
Slice the surface at σ²~within~ = 298.6 and you can see the whole
method: the optimizer walks uphill until the slope is flat.

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Look how flat that peak is**

Everything from roughly 150 to 600 sits within about **one
log-likelihood unit** of the peak. **Variance components are badly
determined with only 16 groups** — and that uncertainty is exactly what
the Kenward-Roger *F*-test accounts for and the Wald χ² ignores.

This plot is the reason those two tests disagreed.
:::
:::
:::::

## Both Routes, One Number {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-reml-03}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
# route 1: moments, from the SS table
moments <- (MS_patch - MS_within) / n

# route 2: maximise the restricted likelihood
fit <- optim(c(200, 300),
             \(p) -reml_ll(p[1], p[2]),
             method = "L-BFGS-B",
             lower = c(0, 1e-6))

# route 3: what lmer() reports
lmer_vc <- as.data.frame(
  VarCorr(u_lmer_model))$vcov[1]

round(c(moments = moments,
        likelihood = fit$par[1],
        lmer = lmer_vc), 3)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**294.31, three ways.**

They agree to within **0.001** — and the first two have **nothing in
common** methodologically. One is algebra on a table of sums of
squares; the other is a numerical search over a likelihood surface.

On a **balanced** design the restricted maximum-likelihood solution has
a closed form, and that closed form *is* the moment estimator — as long
as it comes out positive.
:::

So the traditional route was never wrong. It was a special case that
happens to have a shortcut — and you have been using the shortcut without being told it
was one.

**Next slide: what happens when the shortcut stops existing.**
:::
:::::

## Where the Two Routes Part Company {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
**1. The moment estimator can return a negative variance.**

$MS_{patch} < MS_{within}$ is perfectly possible by chance, and then
$(MS_{patch}-MS_{within})/n$ is **below zero** — an impossible value for
a variance.

```{r lmm-reml-04}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
set.seed(11)
fake <- expand_grid(treat = factor(1:4), p_in = 1:4, quad = 1:5) %>%
  mutate(patch = factor(paste0(treat, "_", p_in)),
         y = rnorm(n(), 10, 5))          # patches truly identical

ft <- summary(aov(y ~ treat + treat:patch, fake))[[1]]
fm <- lmer(y ~ treat + (1 | patch), fake,
           control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

round(c(moments = (ft[2, "Mean Sq"] - ft[3, "Mean Sq"]) / 5,
        REML    = as.data.frame(VarCorr(fm))$vcov[1]), 3)
```

REML cannot go below zero — the likelihood is only defined for
non-negative variances — so it stops at the boundary and warns
**"boundary (singular) fit"**.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**2. Unbalanced data has no single *n* to divide by.**

Thin four patches to one quadrat each, as a storm would:

```{r lmm-reml-05}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
thin <- u_df %>% filter(!(patch %in% c(2, 6, 10, 14) & quad > 1))
tt <- summary(aov(algae ~ treat + treat:patch, thin))[[1]]
tm <- lmer(algae ~ treat + (1 | patch), thin,
           control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

MSp <- tt[2, "Mean Sq"]; MSw <- tt[3, "Mean Sq"]
round(c(`moments, n = 5`    = (MSp - MSw) / 5,
        `moments, n0 = 3.95` = (MSp - MSw) / 3.95,
        REML                 = as.data.frame(VarCorr(tm))$vcov[1]), 1)
```

::: callout-important
Three answers, and the moment estimator needs you to **choose** an
effective *n* before it will give one at all. REML never asks — the
likelihood already knows how many quadrats each patch has.

**This is why mixed models replaced `Error()`.**
:::
:::
:::::

## Why REML and Not Plain ML {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-reml-06}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
ml_fit <- lmer(algae ~ treat + (1 | patch),
               data = u_df, REML = FALSE,
               control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

round(c(
  REML = as.data.frame(VarCorr(u_lmer_model))$vcov[1],
  ML   = as.data.frame(VarCorr(ml_fit))$vcov[1]), 1)
```

Plain maximum likelihood estimates σ²~patch~ as **205.8**. REML gets
**294.3**. ML is biased **30% low**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
You have met this bias before, in week 2.

$$s^2 = \frac{\sum(y-\bar y)^2}{n-\mathbf{1}} \quad\text{not}\quad \frac{\sum(y-\bar y)^2}{n}$$

Dividing by *n* under-estimates the variance because you spent one df
estimating $\bar y$. **ML makes exactly that mistake**, at scale: it
estimates the four treatment means and then behaves as though they were
known all along.

::: callout-important
**REML = "restricted"**: it maximises the likelihood of the data
*after* the fixed effects have been projected out — the
$\log|\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}|$ term three slides back.
That term **is** the $n-1$ correction, generalised.
:::

**Use REML for variance components. Switch to ML only to compare models
with different fixed effects.**
:::
:::::

## Part 4 — The Short Version

::: {.compact-table}
| | **Nested ANOVA (Part 1)** | **Mixed model (Parts 2–7)** |
|------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| Starts from | the total sum of squares | the variance matrix $\mathbf{V}$ |
| Core move | **partition** SS by source | **search** for the most likely variances |
| Variance components from | solving $E[MS]$ equations | maximising the restricted likelihood |
| Needs balance? | **yes**, for exact tests | no |
| Negative variance | can happen, is meaningless | impossible — stops at 0 |
| Unbalanced *n* | you must pick an effective *n* | handled automatically |
| On this dataset | σ²~patch~ = 294.31 | σ²~patch~ = 294.31 |
:::

::: callout-note
**✅ The one sentence**

Sums of squares *divide up* variation that has already been computed;
likelihood *proposes* variances and asks how well they explain the data.
On a balanced design the two land on the same number — everywhere else,
only the second one still works.
:::

## Part 5 · What the Random Effect Buys You {.divider}

## The Intraclass Correlation {.tight-code}

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-04b}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(u_lmer_model))
v_patch <- vc$vcov[vc$grp != "Residual"]
v_resid <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Residual"]

round(c(among_patches  = v_patch,
        within_patches = v_resid,
        ICC = v_patch / (v_patch + v_resid)), 3)
```

Take square roots to get units you can picture: two patches given the
**same** treatment typically differ by **17 points of cover**, and so do
two quadrats in one patch.

The **ICC** is the share of variance living *between* groups —
equivalently, **how strongly two quadrats in the same patch resemble
each other**.
::::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**ICC = 0.50 is the whole reason we are here**

Two quadrats from the same patch are **half-correlated**. They are not
two independent observations.

An ICC near 0 would mean patches barely matter and ordinary ANOVA would
have been fine. An ICC of 0.50 means ignoring patch would have been
badly wrong — and Part 1's naive model showed exactly how wrong
(*F* = 16.11 instead of 2.72).
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Use it to design the next study**

With ICC = 0.50, a sixth quadrat in an existing patch buys you almost
nothing. A **new patch** buys you a lot. The *p*-value could never have
told you that.
:::
::::
:::::::

## The ICC, Said Four Ways {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
$$ICC = \frac{\sigma^2_{among\ groups}}{\sigma^2_{among\ groups} + \sigma^2_{within\ groups}}$$

```{r lmm-icc-02}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
icc  <- v_patch / (v_patch + v_resid)
deff <- 1 + (5 - 1) * icc     # 5 quadrats per patch
# the same model with treatment left out
vc0 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(
  lmer(algae ~ 1 + (1 | patch), data = u_df)))
round(c(ICC = icc, design_effect = deff,
        effective_n = 80 / deff,
        ICC_no_treat = vc0$vcov[1] / sum(vc0$vcov)), 2)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
1. **A share of variance** — half the leftover variation is
   patch-to-patch, half is quadrat-to-quadrat.
2. **A correlation** — two quadrats from the same patch are correlated
   at *r* = 0.50. (Hence the name: **i**ntra**c**lass **c**orrelation.)
3. **Redundancy** — a second quadrat in a patch is half new
   information, half something you already knew.
4. **Lost sample size** — the *design effect* 1 + (*m* − 1) × ICC says
   80 quadrats carry the information of about **27** independent ones.

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ What people get wrong**

A **small** ICC still bites when groups are big: 0.05 with 100 fish
per lake is a design effect of 5.95. And it depends on the fixed
effects: 0.50 with treatment in the model, 0.58 without.
:::
:::
:::::

## Price the Next Experiment {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
The two variances give the standard error of a treatment mean for
**any** design, before you get wet:

$$SE = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2_{patch}}{\text{patches}} + \frac{\sigma^2_{within}}{\text{patches} \times \text{quadrats}}}$$

```{r lmm-design-01}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
se_mean <- function(patches, quads) {
  sqrt(v_patch / patches + v_resid / (patches * quads))
}

round(c(done_4x5    = se_mean(4, 5),
        quads_4x20  = se_mean(4, 20),
        patch_8x5   = se_mean(8, 5)), 2)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**More quadrats: 9.41 → 8.79. More patches: 9.41 → 6.65.**

Four times the quadrat work buys almost nothing. Twice the patches —
with *half* that work — buys a lot. With 4 patches you can never get
below $\sqrt{294.3 / 4}$ = 8.58, however many quadrats you count.
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 This is what *p* = 0.091 meant**

**83%** of the uncertainty in a treatment mean came from having only
four patches. The experiment was not short of data. It was short of
**patches**.
:::
:::
:::::

## Three Ways to Estimate a Group {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
"Pooling" just means **sharing data across groups**. What is the true
mean of one patch?

::: {.compact-table}
| | What you do | In R |
|-----------|---------------------------|----------------|
| **Complete pooling** | ignore patch; every patch gets its treatment mean | `lm(algae ~ treat)` |
| **No pooling** | every patch gets its own raw mean of 5 quadrats | `lm(algae ~ patch)` |
| **Partial pooling** | a weighted compromise between the two | `lmer(... + (1|patch))` |
:::

$$\text{weight} = \frac{\sigma^2_{patch}}{\sigma^2_{patch} + \sigma^2_{within} / n}$$

$$\text{estimate} = \text{treatment mean} + \text{weight} \times (\text{raw mean} - \text{treatment mean})$$

Weight 1 = believe the patch's own mean. Weight 0 = ignore it.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r lmm-pool-01}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
w <- v_patch / (v_patch + v_resid / 5)
round(w, 2)

u_df %>%
  group_by(treat, patch) %>%
  summarise(raw = mean(algae), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(treat) %>%
  mutate(trt_mean = mean(raw),
         model = trt_mean + w * (raw - trt_mean)) %>%
  filter(treat == "0%") %>%
  mutate(model = round(model, 1)) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```

::: callout-note
**📖 Read the weight as two kinds of doubt**

Patches really differ a lot (big σ²~patch~) → trust each patch.
Quadrats are noisy or few (big σ²~within~ / *n*) → trust it less.
Nobody picks the weight; it follows from the two variances.
:::
:::
:::::

## Partial Pooling — What Happens to Each Patch

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
A random effect does not just adjust the *p*-value. It changes each
patch's **estimate**.

```{r linear-mixed-models-04c}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.2
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: "Slope plot comparing each patch's raw observed mean algae cover to its shrunken mixed-model estimate, with lines joining the two; estimates move toward their treatment mean, and patches with more extreme raw means move furthest."
raw_means <- u_df %>%
  group_by(treat, patch) %>%
  summarise(raw = mean(algae), .groups = "drop")

raw_means$fitted <- predict(u_lmer_model,
                            newdata = raw_means[, c("treat", "patch")])

raw_means %>%
  pivot_longer(c(raw, fitted), names_to = "kind", values_to = "algae") %>%
  mutate(kind = factor(kind, c("raw", "fitted"),
                       c("raw patch mean", "model estimate"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(kind, algae, group = patch, color = treat)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Algae cover (%)", color = "Treatment") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 New word: shrinkage**

Every patch estimate is pulled **toward its treatment mean**. The model
treats an extreme patch average as partly real signal and partly luck,
and splits the difference.

Patches with fewer quadrats, or more internal scatter, get pulled
further.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Why this is a feature**

A patch whose 5 quadrats happened to land high is probably *not* that
extreme — the next 5 would come back closer to average.

This is **partial pooling**: between treating every patch as unrelated
and pretending they are all identical.
:::
::::
:::::::

## Shrinkage, With the Right Answer Visible

::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r lmm-shrink-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-alt: "Twelve simulated lakes sorted by number of fish caught, from two to eighty. For each lake a grey dot shows the raw average mass, a blue dot the mixed-model estimate and a black cross the true mean, with an arrow from grey to blue. Arrows are long for lakes with few fish and absent for lakes with many, and all point toward the vertical line marking the all-lakes mean."
set.seed(2026)
sh_n <- c(2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 20, 40, 80)   # fish netted per lake

sh_survey <- function() {
  truth <- rnorm(12, 450, 40)                        # lakes differ: SD 40 g
  d <- tibble(lake = factor(rep(1:12, sh_n)),
              true_mean = rep(truth, sh_n),
              mass = true_mean + rnorm(sum(sh_n), 0, 80))   # fish: SD 80 g
  m <- suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(
    lmer(mass ~ 1 + (1 | lake), data = d)))
  d %>%
    group_by(lake) %>%
    summarise(n = n(), true_mean = first(true_mean),
              raw = mean(mass), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(model = coef(m)$lake[as.character(lake), 1],
           grand = fixef(m)[1],
           sd_lake = sqrt(as.numeric(VarCorr(m)$lake)))
}

# draw surveys until one estimates the lake SD close to its true 40 g,
# so the picture shows a typical survey rather than a lucky or unlucky one
repeat {
  sh_one <- sh_survey()
  if (abs(sh_one$sd_lake[1] - 40) < 5) break
}
sh_closer <- sum(abs(sh_one$model - sh_one$true_mean) <
                   abs(sh_one$raw - sh_one$true_mean))

sh_one %>%
  mutate(lab = fct_rev(fct_inorder(paste0("lake ", lake, "  (n = ", n, ")")))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = lab)) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = grand), colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = raw, xend = model, yend = lab), colour = "grey40",
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) +
  geom_point(aes(x = raw, shape = "raw lake average"),
             colour = "grey55", size = 2.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = model, shape = "mixed-model estimate"),
             colour = "#0072B2", size = 2.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = true_mean, shape = "TRUTH"), size = 2.8, stroke = 1.1) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c("raw lake average" = 16, "mixed-model estimate" = 16, "TRUTH" = 4),
    breaks = c("raw lake average", "mixed-model estimate", "TRUTH"), name = NULL,
    guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(
      colour = c("grey55", "#0072B2", "black")))) +
  labs(x = "Mean trout mass (g)", y = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
Twelve made-up lakes where we **know** each lake's true mean trout
mass. We net 2 fish in some and 80 in others, then fit
`lmer(mass ~ 1 + (1 | lake))`.

- **Long arrows at the top, none at the bottom.** The model moves the
  lakes it has reason to doubt, toward the all-lakes mean (orange).
- The most extreme raw averages are mostly **small samples**. That is
  regression to the mean.

::: callout-important
**In this survey the model was closer to the truth in
`{r} sh_closer` of 12 lakes**

Not all 12. A truly exceptional lake gets pulled in too. Shrinkage is
a bet that pays **on average**.
:::
:::
:::::

## Does the Bet Pay Off?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r lmm-shrink-02}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-alt: "Typical error of three estimates of a lake's true mean against number of fish caught, from five hundred simulated surveys. The raw lake average has large error at two fish and falls steeply; the grand mean has constant error near forty grams; the mixed-model estimate lies below both at every sample size and merges with the raw average by eighty fish."
sh_many <- map_dfr(1:500, \(i) sh_survey())

sh_rmse <- sh_many %>%
  group_by(n) %>%
  summarise(`No pooling: raw lake average` =
              sqrt(mean((raw - true_mean)^2)),
            `Complete pooling: grand mean for all` =
              sqrt(mean((grand - true_mean)^2)),
            `Partial pooling: mixed model` =
              sqrt(mean((model - true_mean)^2)), .groups = "drop")

sh_all <- round(c(raw   = sqrt(mean((sh_many$raw   - sh_many$true_mean)^2)),
                  model = sqrt(mean((sh_many$model - sh_many$true_mean)^2))))

sh_rmse %>%
  pivot_longer(-n) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20, 40, 80)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "grey55", "#0072B2"), name = NULL) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(x = "Fish caught in the lake (log scale)",
       y = "Typical error in the lake's mean (g)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.98, 0.98),
        legend.justification = c(1, 1), legend.text = element_text(size = 7.5))
```
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
The same survey, repeated 500 times. Lower is better.

- With **2 fish**, the raw average is the worst estimate on the page.
  With **80**, raw and mixed model are the same thing.
- The mixed model is **never worse than either alternative**.

Across all lakes the typical error falls from
**`{r} sh_all["raw"]` g to `{r} sh_all["model"]` g**.

::: callout-note
**📖 "Borrowing strength"**

A lake with 2 fish is estimated using what the other 11 lakes taught
the model about **how much lakes differ**. It matters whenever the
groups themselves are the point: ranking sites, or predicting for one
lake. Raw rankings put small samples at both ends of the list.
:::
:::
:::::

## Reporting the Variance Components

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: callout-note
**How to report this result**

"Algal cover did not differ significantly among urchin density
treatments (linear mixed model with patch as a random effect,
***F*~3,12~ = 2.72, *p* = 0.091**, Kenward-Roger denominator df).
Among-patch variance was substantial (**σ²~patch~ = 294.3** vs
**σ²~within~ = 298.6**, ICC = 0.50), indicating strong spatial
heterogeneity in algal cover."
:::

Both halves belong in the sentence. The fixed effect answers *did the
treatment do anything*; the variance component answers *how noisy is
this reef*, which is what the next person planning a study needs.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**⚠️ "Not significant" is not "no effect"**

With σ²~patch~ ≈ σ²~within~, patch-to-patch variation is as large as
quadrat-to-quadrat variation. Four patches per treatment simply cannot
resolve a treatment effect against that much background noise.

The honest conclusion is **"this design could not detect it"**, not
"urchins do not affect algae."
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Where 294.3 came from**

By hand from the mean squares, from a restricted likelihood maximised
with `optim()`, and from `VarCorr()` — three routes, one number.
See Part 4.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 6 · Post-Hoc, Assumptions, and Reporting {.divider}

## Estimated Marginal Means {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-09}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
u_emm <- emmeans(u_lmer_model, ~ treat)
u_emm
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
Every standard error is **9.41** — identical across treatments, because
the design is balanced and the SE comes from the **patch** stratum
(4 patches per treatment), not from the 20 quadrats.

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Two of these intervals go below zero**

Algae cover is a percentage. It cannot be negative.

The mixed model fixed the **error structure** and left the
**distribution** alone — it still assumes normal, unbounded response.
Last week you fixed the distribution and left the error structure alone.
Real data often needs both: that is `glmer()`.
:::
:::
:::::

## Post-Hoc Comparisons {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-11}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
multcomp::cld(u_emm, alpha = 0.05, Letters = letters)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**Every treatment shares the letter `a`.**

No pair is distinguishable. That is the correct and expected result —
the omnibus *F*-test was already non-significant (*p* = 0.091), so there
was nothing for a post-hoc to find.

Running post-hocs after a non-significant omnibus test is **exploratory
only**. Report it as such, or not at all.
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 Read the pattern, not a ranking**

The means run 39.2 → 19.0 → 21.6 → 1.3. The two middle treatments are
effectively tied, so this is **not** a clean monotonic gradient. Resist
the temptation to write one.
:::
:::
:::::

## Diagnostics 1 — `check_model()` First {.tight-code}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-12}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.0
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-alt: "The performance package's check_model output for the urchin mixed model, with three panels: a normal Q-Q plot of the residuals whose tails bend away from the line, a Q-Q plot of the sixteen patch random effects which sit close to their line, and a homogeneity-of-variance panel whose trend rises from left to right."
check_model(u_lmer_model,
            check = c("qq", "reqq", "homogeneity"))
```
:::

::::: {.column width="44%"}
The same one call as every other model this term — and on a `merMod` it
adds a panel you have not seen before.

::: callout-note
**📖 The `reqq` panel is the new one**

A mixed model assumes **two** things are normal: the residuals *and the
random effects*. `reqq` is a Q-Q plot of the 16 patch intercepts, and it
is the only diagnostic here that looks at them.

```{r lmm-diag-01}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
check_normality(u_lmer_model,
                effects = "random")
```

Reassuring — but it is 16 numbers. Report it, and say that 16 levels
cannot carry a strong claim either way.
:::
:::::
::::::

## Diagnostics 2 — Why Those Residual Tests Mislead {.tight-code}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-diag-02}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
check_normality(u_lmer_model)

check_heteroscedasticity(u_lmer_model)
```

Both scream *p* < .001. **Neither number means what it would mean for an
`lm()`.**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**⚠️ The reference distribution is wrong**

Those tests ask: *are these residuals iid normal with constant
variance?* For an `lm()` that **is** the assumption. For a mixed model
it is **not**:

- Conditional residuals are **shrunk** toward zero by partial pooling,
  so they are not even supposed to have variance σ²~within~
- How much each one shrinks depends on its patch's *n* and the ICC
- So a non-normal, non-constant-variance pattern is partly **what the
  model does on purpose**

Shapiro and Breusch–Pagan have no way to know that. They compare your
residuals against a yardstick that does not apply.
:::
:::
::::::

## Diagnostics 3 — DHARMa Builds the Right Yardstick {.tight-code}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Instead of assuming a reference distribution, **simulate** it from the
fitted model:

```{r lmm-diag-03}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.0
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-alt: "DHARMa diagnostic output for the urchin mixed model: a Q-Q plot of scaled residuals against a uniform reference with the KS, dispersion and outlier test results printed on it, beside a plot of scaled residuals against predicted values with quantile regression lines."
set.seed(42)
sim <- simulateResiduals(u_lmer_model, n = 1000)
plot(sim)
```

1. Simulate 1000 new datasets from the fitted model
2. For each observation, ask **what quantile of its own simulated
   distribution** the real value sits at
3. Under a correct model those quantiles are **Uniform(0, 1)** — always
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**✅ Why this is better**

The yardstick is **generated by your model**, so it already contains the
shrinkage, the unequal group sizes, the ICC — everything that broke the
tests on the last slide.

And "should be uniform" holds for **any** model: `lmer`, `glmer`,
Poisson, negative binomial, zero-inflated. You learn **one** diagnostic
instead of one per family.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Keep `check_model()` anyway**

It is faster to read, and `reqq` is genuinely useful. Use it to **look**,
and DHARMa to **decide**.
:::
:::
::::::

## Diagnostics 4 — What DHARMa Actually Concluded {.tight-code}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r lmm-diag-04}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
testUniformity(sim, plot = FALSE)$p.value

testDispersion(sim, plot = FALSE)$p.value

testOutliers(sim, plot = FALSE)$p.value
```

```{r lmm-diag-05}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
# test at the level of the experimental unit
sim_patch <- recalculateResiduals(
  sim, group = u_df$patch)

testUniformity(sim_patch, plot = FALSE)$p.value
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.compact-table}
| Test | *p* | Verdict |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Shapiro, residuals | **< 0.001** | wrong yardstick |
| Breusch–Pagan | **< 0.001** | wrong yardstick |
| DHARMa uniformity | **0.022** | mild deviation |
| DHARMa dispersion | **0.64** | fine |
| DHARMa outliers | **1.00** | none |
| DHARMa, by patch | **0.092** | fine |
:::

::: callout-important
**The honest summary changed**

Not "this model fails two assumptions at *p* < 0.001". It is **"a mild
distributional deviation, no dispersion problem, no outliers, and
nothing wrong at the level of the 16 patches."**

Same model, same data. The second description is the defensible one.
:::

**`recalculateResiduals(group =)`** is the mixed-model-specific move:
the treatment was applied to **patches**, so test there too.
:::
::::::

## Heterogeneity of Variance {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-13}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
leveneTest(algae ~ treat, data = u_df)
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ This test ignores `patch`**

`leveneTest()` has no idea the quadrats are grouped. It is testing the
80 raw values as if they were independent — the very assumption this
whole lecture exists to fix. Read it as a **description** of the raw
spread, not as a test of the mixed model.

The model's own diagnostic is the residuals-vs-fitted plot, and DHARMa.
:::

Variances really are unequal (the 100% treatment has SD 3.2, the 0%
treatment 28.7). Quinn & Keough noted the same thing, tried
transformations including arcsine, and found none that fixed it — so
they analysed the untransformed data and said so. A balanced ANOVA is
reasonably robust to this. **Say it out loud in the methods rather than
hoping nobody checks.**
:::
:::::

## Visualization

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-14}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| fig-width: 4.0
#| fig-height: 3.1
#| fig-alt: "Boxplot of algae cover by urchin density treatment with jittered quadrat points overlaid, showing high cover and wide spread in the 0% treatment and near-zero cover in the 100% treatment."
ggplot(u_df, aes(x = treat, y = algae, fill = treat)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.85) +
  labs(x = "Urchin density treatment", y = "Algae cover (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-15}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| fig-width: 4.0
#| fig-height: 3.1
#| fig-alt: "Model estimated marginal means with 95% confidence intervals by treatment, with the sixteen individual patch means plotted behind them, showing the patch means scatter widely within every treatment."
ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = raw_means, aes(treat, raw),
              width = 0.12, alpha = 0.55, size = 2, color = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(data = as.data.frame(u_emm),
                  aes(treat, emmean, ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL),
                  color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8, size = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = "Urchin density treatment", y = "Algae cover (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```

**Grey** — the 16 patch means. **Red** — the model's treatment means and
95% intervals. The grey scatter *within* each treatment is σ²~patch~;
it is why the red intervals are so wide.
:::
:::::

## Part 7 · The Same Factor, Fixed or Random — the Crayfish {.divider}

## Back to the Crayfish {.tight-code}

```{r lmm-cray-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
cray_df <- read_csv("data/sargent_lodge_crayfish.csv",
                    show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(range = factor(range, levels = c("Native", "Invasive")),
         lake  = factor(lake,  levels = c("Big", "High", "Papoose")))

cray_cells <- cray_df %>%
  group_by(lake, range) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(growth_per_day), .groups = "drop")

cray_fixed <- lm(growth_per_day ~ range * lake, data = cray_df)
cray_add   <- lm(growth_per_day ~ range + lake, data = cray_df)
cray_ri    <- lmer(growth_per_day ~ range + (1 | lake), data = cray_df)
cray_rs    <- lmer(growth_per_day ~ range + (1 | lake) + (1 | lake:range),
                   data = cray_df)
```

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Sargent & Lodge (2014). Young-of-year rusty crayfish from the **Native**
(Ohio) and **Invasive** (Wisconsin) range, grown in enclosures in three
Wisconsin lakes. Response: `growth_per_day` (mm/day).

In the factorial weeks `lake` was a **fixed** factor, and the
two-way ANOVA said:

```{r lmm-cray-02}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
Anova(cray_fixed, type = 3)[2:4, ]
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-cray-03}
#| echo: false
#| collapse: true
cray_cells %>%
  dplyr::select(-n) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = range, values_from = mean) %>%
  mutate(advantage = Invasive - Native) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

::: callout-important
**The result you already know**

Invasive crayfish grew **+0.070** mm/day faster in Big, **+0.072** in
High, and **−0.003** in Papoose. The interaction (*p* = 0.000017) *is*
the finding: the advantage is real in two lakes and absent in the third.

Hold on to that. Today's question is what happens to it when `lake`
becomes random.
:::
:::
:::::

## Fixed Lake or Random Lake? Two Different Questions

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.compact-table}
| | `lake` **fixed** (factorial weeks) | `lake` **random** (today) |
|------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| The question | do **Big, High, Papoose** differ? | how much do **lakes** vary? |
| What R estimates | a mean for each lake (2 parameters) | one variance, σ²~lake~ (1 parameter) |
| Post-hoc | Tukey: Big vs Papoose, etc. | **none** — no levels to compare |
| Inference is about | **these three lakes** | lakes **in general**, these three being a sample |
| The interaction | `range:lake`, 2 df, tested | **gone** unless you ask for it (two slides on) |
| `lake` gets a | *p*-value | **variance** and a **standard deviation** |
:::

Neither is "the correct model". They answer different questions, and
the right one is whichever matches the question you would write in the
Discussion.
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-tip
**🖐 Which did the authors mean?**

Sargent & Lodge did not care whether Big Lake differs from High Lake.
They wanted to know whether the invasive-range advantage holds in
Wisconsin lakes **generally** — that is a random-effect question.

The catch: they only had **three** lakes. Keep that number in view for
the rest of this part.
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 Same data, same `options()`**

`contr.sum` is still set from the start of the lecture, so every
coefficient reads the same way it did in the factorial weeks.
:::
::::
:::::::

## `summary()` Line by Line — the Top Half {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r lmm-cray-04}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
cray_ri <- lmer(
  growth_per_day ~ range + (1 | lake),
  data = cray_df)

summary(cray_ri)
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
- **`fit by REML`** — the variances came from the restricted likelihood
  of Part 4, not from a sums-of-squares table. **`Satterthwaite's
  method`** is how the *t*-test df below were approximated.
- **`REML criterion at convergence: −297.6`** — minus twice the
  restricted log-likelihood at the peak. It is not an *R*². Lower is
  better, and it is only comparable between models with the **same
  fixed effects**.
- **`Scaled residuals`** — residuals divided by the residual SD. Centred
  near 0, roughly symmetric; the **Max of 3.64** is the one crayfish
  that grew from 9 to 40 mm — the factorial weeks' outlier, still here.
- **`Random effects`** — the new block. Two rows, no *p*-values: see the
  next slide.
- **`Number of obs: 84, groups: lake, 3`** — the replication for
  anything that varies **between** lakes is 3, not 84.
:::
:::::

## `summary()` Line by Line — the Bottom Half {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r lmm-cray-05}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
print(VarCorr(cray_ri),
      comp = c("Variance", "Std.Dev."))

round(coef(summary(cray_ri)), 4)
```

```{r lmm-cray-06}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
emmeans(cray_ri, pairwise ~ range)$contrasts
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
**Random effects.** `lake (Intercept)` Variance **0.00396**, Std.Dev.
**0.063**; `Residual` Variance 0.00125, Std.Dev. 0.035. Read the SDs —
they are in **mm/day**: lakes typically sit ±0.063 from the average
lake, and crayfish within a lake scatter ±0.035. ICC =
0.00396 / (0.00396 + 0.00125) = **0.76**. There is **no *F*, no df, no
*p*** on this row: `lake` is *described*, not tested.

**`(Intercept)` 0.2529.** Under `contr.sum`, the mean of the two range
means — not the mean of the 84 crayfish (0.255). Its df is **2.0** and
its SE 0.037 is enormous: where "the average lake" sits is known only
from three lakes.

**`range1` −0.0215.** Native's distance from that centre; Invasive sits
+0.0215 the other side, so **Invasive − Native = 0.043 mm/day** — the
contrast confirms it. Its df is **80**: `range` varies *within* every
lake, so every crayfish counts (84 − 1 − 3 = 80).

**`Correlation of Fixed Effects`.** Between the *estimates*, not the
data. Ignore it unless it is near ±1.
:::
:::::

## Three Models, One Row Each {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-cray-07}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
a_int <- Anova(cray_fixed, type = 3)["range", ]
a_add <- Anova(cray_add,   type = 3)["range", ]
a_ri  <- Anova(cray_ri, type = 3,
               test.statistic = "F")["range", ]

tibble(
  model = c("range * lake, fixed",
            "range + lake, fixed",
            "range + (1 | lake)"),
  F     = c(a_int$`F value`, a_add$`F value`, a_ri$F),
  df2   = c(df.residual(cray_fixed),
            df.residual(cray_add), a_ri$Df.res),
  p     = c(a_int$`Pr(>F)`, a_add$`Pr(>F)`,
            a_ri$`Pr(>F)`))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**The random intercept changed nothing about `range`**

The additive fixed model and the random-intercept model give
***F* = 27.6 on 1 and 80 df** — the same test, to the second decimal.
Making `lake` random did not buy a better *p*-value. It changed **how
`lake` is reported** (one variance instead of two means) and **what you
may generalise to**.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ And it quietly dropped a row**

The top model has an interaction. The other two do not. The
random-intercept model is **the additive model** — it assumes the
invasive advantage is the same in every lake.

The factorial weeks showed that assumption is **false** (*p* =
0.000017).
:::
:::
:::::

## Where Did the Interaction Go?

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r lmm-cray-08}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-alt: "Two panels of growth per day against range with one line per lake. Left, random intercept only: three parallel lines. Right, random intercept and slope: Big and High rise steeply while Papoose is flat. Observed cell means are overlaid as points in both panels."
nd <- expand.grid(range = levels(cray_df$range),
                  lake  = levels(cray_df$lake))
nd$`(1 | lake)`               <- predict(cray_ri, newdata = nd)
nd$`(1 | lake) + (1 | lake:range)` <- predict(cray_rs, newdata = nd)

nd %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(range, lake), names_to = "model", values_to = "fit") %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model, c("(1 | lake)",
                                 "(1 | lake) + (1 | lake:range)"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(range, fit, group = lake, color = lake)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = cray_cells %>%
               tidyr::crossing(model = factor(c("(1 | lake)",
                                 "(1 | lake) + (1 | lake:range)"))),
             aes(y = mean), shape = 1, size = 2.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Growth (mm/day)", color = "Lake") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Open circles are the observed cell means. The left model cannot reach
Papoose's two points: it is only allowed to move each lake **up or
down**, so the invasive advantage is forced to be the same everywhere.
::::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**`(1 | lake)` = parallel lines**

A random **intercept** gives every lake its own baseline and **nothing
else**. That is exactly "no interaction".
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Pseudoreplication, in a new costume**

The thing we want to generalise is *the invasive advantage in a lake*.
That is observed **three times**. Yet the random-intercept model tests
`range` on **80 df**, as if every crayfish were an independent
replicate of it — the same mistake Part 1 priced at *F* = 16.11 instead
of 2.72.
:::
::::
:::::::

## Random Intercepts *and* Random Slopes {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-cray-09}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
cray_rs <- lmer(
  growth_per_day ~ range +
    (1 | lake) + (1 | lake:range),
  data = cray_df)

VarCorr(cray_rs)

Anova(cray_rs, type = 3,
      test.statistic = "F")["range", ]

emmeans(cray_rs, pairwise ~ range)$contrasts
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
`(1 | lake:range)` gives **each lake its own range effect** — a random
*slope* for `range`, spelled as a random intercept on the six
lake-by-range cells. The right-hand panel of the previous slide.

- **`lake:range` SD 0.030 mm/day** — how much the invasive advantage
  wobbles from lake to lake. The interaction row, as a variance.
- ***F*~1,2~ = 3.3, *p* = 0.21.** The estimate is still **0.046**, but
  the SE went from 0.008 to **0.025** and the df from 80 to **2**.

::: callout-important
**The yardstick changed**

`range` is now tested against **lake-to-lake disagreement about the
advantage**, on 3 − 1 = 2 df. One lake in three dissents, so the
advantage is not reliably general. That is the honest answer to the
general question.
:::
:::
:::::

## The Other Spelling: `(1 + range | lake)` {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-cray-10}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
#| warning: true
cray_rs_corr <- lmer(
  growth_per_day ~ range + (1 + range | lake),
  data = cray_df)

VarCorr(cray_rs_corr)

Anova(cray_rs_corr, type = 3,
      test.statistic = "F")["range", ]
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
This is the textbook random-slope formula, and it is the same idea with
one extra parameter: the **correlation** between a lake's intercept and
its slope (do high-growth lakes also show a bigger advantage?).

- Same ***F* ≈ 3.2 on 2 df, *p* ≈ 0.22** — the conclusion does not move.
- But the correlation is **−1.00** and R warns **`boundary (singular)
  fit`**. Three lakes cannot estimate a correlation; the optimiser hit
  the edge, exactly as in Part 4.

::: callout-tip
**🖐 The rule**

Reach for `(1 + x | g)` when `x` is **continuous** or you have many
groups. For a factor with few groups, `(1 | g) + (1 | g:x)` asks the
same question with one fewer parameter and no singular fit. The
[Mixed Model Structures](../../vignettes/16_mixed_model_structures_vignette/mixed_model_structures.qmd)
page works through both.
:::
:::
:::::

## Which Analysis Is Right? Whichever Matches the Question

::: {.compact-table}
+----------------------------------+------------------+------------------------------------------------------------+
| Model                            | `range` *p*      | What you may write in the Discussion                       |
+==================================+==================+============================================================+
| `range * lake`, all fixed        | < 0.0001, **but  | "In Big and High Lake invasive crayfish grew ~0.07 mm/day  |
|                                  | the interaction  | faster; in Papoose they did not." Strong, specific, true — |
|                                  | rules**          | **about these three lakes.**                               |
+----------------------------------+------------------+------------------------------------------------------------+
| `range + (1 | lake)`             | 0.000001         | "Invasive crayfish grow faster in lakes generally" —       |
|                                  |                  | **only by assuming the advantage is the same in every      |
|                                  |                  | lake**, which the data contradict. Do not write this.      |
+----------------------------------+------------------+------------------------------------------------------------+
| `range + (1 | lake) +`           | 0.21             | "Across lakes generally, we cannot say the advantage       |
| `(1 | lake:range)`               |                  | holds: it appeared in two of three lakes." Honest, weak —  |
|                                  |                  | because **three lakes is three replicates.**               |
+----------------------------------+------------------+------------------------------------------------------------+
:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**The advantage of the mixed model is not a smaller *p***

It is that it makes you **say what you are generalising to**, and then
prices it. The fixed model answers the within-study question perfectly.
The random-slope model answers the general question honestly: *not yet
known*.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ What "three levels is too few" looks like**

`confint(cray_ri)` puts σ~lake~ between **0.027 and 0.152** — a
six-fold range. The variance you are reporting is barely estimated.
With 16 patches (Parts 1–6) the random effect was the right tool. With
3 lakes it is a demonstration, and the fixed model is the one to report.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 7 — The Short Version

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
1. A fixed factor gives you **its levels**; a random factor gives you
   **a variance**. Choose by the question, not by the data.
2. `(1 | g)` is **parallel lines** — a random intercept assumes the
   treatment effect is identical in every group. That is the additive
   model, and it tests the treatment on within-group df.
3. A random **slope** — `(1 | g) + (1 | g:x)` or `(1 + x | g)` — lets
   the treatment effect vary by group. It is the interaction, as a
   variance, and it tests the treatment on **group** df.
4. Few groups → the variance is poorly estimated, the random slope has
   almost no df, and `(1 + x | g)` goes singular. **Below ~5 levels,
   fit the factor as fixed** and say the generalisation rests on *k*
   groups.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 In one sentence**

The mixed model did not change the crayfish result. It changed **who
the result is about** — and showed that the general claim is carried by
three lakes, two of which agree.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 8 · Two Designs You Will Actually Run {.divider}

## Animals Followed Through Time — Chick Growth

::::: columns
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r lmm-chick-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Body weight against age in days for fifty chicks, one line per chick, in four panels by diet. Lines start close together near forty grams and fan out with age; diet 3 chicks reach the highest weights."
ck_df <- as_tibble(ChickWeight) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(chick = factor(chick, ordered = FALSE))

ggplot(ck_df, aes(time, weight, group = chick)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ diet, nrow = 1, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Age (days)", y = "Body weight (g)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

`ChickWeight` ships with R: **50 chicks** on **4 diets**, each weighed
up to **12 times** over 21 days — 578 weighings.
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
Same structure as the urchins, turned on its side:

::: {.compact-table}
| Urchins | Chicks |
|------------------|------------------|
| treatment → patch | diet → chick |
| 5 quadrats per patch | 12 weighings per chick |
| 16 patches | 50 chicks |
:::

The diet was given to the **chick**. Twelve weighings of one chick are
not twelve chicks.

::: callout-note
**📖 What is new**

Time is a predictor **inside** each chick, so each chick has its own
**line** — its own starting weight and its own growth rate. That is a
random intercept **and** a random slope:

`weight ~ time * diet + (1 + time | chick)`
:::
:::
:::::

## Each Chick Gets Its Own Growth Line {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="54%"}
The question is `time:diet` — **do chicks grow at different rates on
different diets?**

```{r lmm-chick-02}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
ck_lm <- lm(weight ~ time * diet, data = ck_df)
ck_ri <- lmer(weight ~ time * diet + (1 | chick),
              data = ck_df)
ck_rs <- lmer(weight ~ time * diet + (1 + time | chick),
              data = ck_df)
```

```{r lmm-chick-03}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
a_lm <- car::Anova(ck_lm, type = 3)
a_ri <- anova(ck_ri)
a_rs <- anova(ck_rs)

data.frame(
  model   = c("lm, no chick", "(1 | chick)", "(1 + time | chick)"),
  F_value = round(c(a_lm["time:diet", "F value"],
                    a_ri["time:diet", "F value"],
                    a_rs["time:diet", "F value"]), 1),
  den_df  = round(c(a_lm["Residuals", "Df"],
                    a_ri["time:diet", "DenDF"],
                    a_rs["time:diet", "DenDF"])))
```
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
::: callout-important
**570 → 527 → 46**

Only the last row knows there are **50 chicks**. The first two test a
growth-rate difference against the wobble of single weighings.

Growth rate belongs to a chick, so it must be tested against
**chick-to-chick variation in growth rate**. Diet still matters
(*p* = 0.002) — on honest df.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ The random intercept made it worse**

`(1 | chick)` gave the **largest** *F*. It removed the differences
between chicks from the noise, while still assuming every chick on a
