diet grows at the same rate.

If the effect of a predictor can differ among your animals, it needs
the **random slope**.
:::
:::
:::::

## What the Chick Model Says {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r lmm-chick-04}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
VarCorr(ck_rs)

emtrends(ck_rs, ~ diet, var = "time") %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  dplyr::select(diet, time.trend, SE, df) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
Read the random effects as biology:

- **`time` SD 3.3** — chicks on the *same* diet differ in growth rate
  by about 3.3 g/day. Against a mean of 6–11 g/day, individuals vary a
  lot.
- **Residual 12.8** — one weighing sits about 13 g off that chick's own
  line.
- **Corr −0.98** — do not interpret it. Growth curves upward, so a
  straight line through a fast grower starts too low.

::: callout-note
**📖 `emtrends()` is `emmeans()` for slopes**

Growth is **6.3 g/day** on diet 1 and **11.4** on diet 3. Each SE rests
on about 45 df — the chicks.
:::

**Your own time series** — tagged fish, resurveyed plots, repeat blood
samples — is the same model: `(1 + time | id)`.
:::
:::::

## What a Random Slope Does to the Spread

::::: columns
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r lmm-chick-05}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-alt: "Standard deviation of body weight among chicks on the same diet against age. The observed spread rises from about one gram at hatching to about sixty grams at day twenty-one. The random-intercept model implies a flat line; the random-slope model implies a rising curve close to the observed one from day ten onward."
ck_obs <- ck_df %>%
  group_by(diet, time) %>%
  summarise(v = var(weight), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  summarise(sd = sqrt(mean(v)), .groups = "drop")

ck_G  <- as.matrix(Matrix::bdiag(VarCorr(ck_rs)))     # 2 x 2: intercept, slope
ck_s2 <- sigma(ck_rs)^2

ck_sd <- ck_obs %>%
  transmute(time,
            `Observed` = sd,
            `(1 | chick)` = sqrt(as.numeric(VarCorr(ck_ri)$chick) +
                                   sigma(ck_ri)^2),
            `(1 + time | chick)` = sqrt(ck_G[1, 1] + 2 * time * ck_G[1, 2] +
                                          time^2 * ck_G[2, 2] + ck_s2))

ck_sd %>%
  pivot_longer(-time) %>%
  mutate(name = fct_inorder(name)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(time, value, colour = name, linetype = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "grey55", "#0072B2"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "solid"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Age (days)", y = "SD among chicks on one diet (g)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
Chicks hatch almost identical and end up very different. **The spread
among animals grows through time.**

Each formula is a claim about that spread:

- **`(1 | chick)`** — chicks differ by a constant amount at every age.
  A flat line; parallel growth curves.
- **`(1 + time | chick)`** — chicks differ in growth **rate**, so they
  fan out. (It is still too wide at hatching: one residual variance
  has to serve every age.)

$$\sigma^2_{age} = \sigma^2_{int} + 2 \cdot age \cdot cov + age^2 \cdot \sigma^2_{slope} + \sigma^2_{resid}$$

::: callout-tip
**🖐 How to choose, before any test**

Plot one line per animal. **Parallel** → random intercept.
**Fanning, crossing or converging** → random slope.
:::
:::
:::::

## A Treatment Blocked by Stream

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r lmm-stream-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-alt: "Insects per sample on a log scale for three reach types, reference, willow and removed, in three panels, one per stream. Grey dots are the fifteen samples in each reach and blue diamonds joined by a line are the nine reach means. All three streams drop from reference to willow, but the streams sit at different overall levels."
w_df <- read_csv("data/willow_streams_simulated.csv",
                 show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(reach  = factor(reach, levels = c("reference", "willow", "removed")),
         stream = factor(stream),
         log_insects = log(insects))

w_means <- w_df %>%
  group_by(stream, reach) %>%
  summarise(log_insects = mean(log_insects), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(w_df, aes(reach, log_insects)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey55", alpha = 0.6, size = 1,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  geom_line(data = w_means, aes(group = stream), colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(data = w_means, colour = "#0072B2", size = 3, shape = 18) +
  facet_wrap(~ stream, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log(insects per sample)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**3 streams.** In each: a **reference** reach, a reach with **crack
willow**, and a reach where willow was **removed**. **15 benthic
samples** per reach — 135 in all.

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ These data are simulated**

The layout is a real student project; the numbers are invented, so we
know the truth: willow cuts insects by 30%.
:::

::: callout-important
**Ask the giveaway question again**

*What was the treatment applied to?* A **reach**. There are **9**
reaches — the blue diamonds — and only **3 of each kind**, one per
stream.

The 15 samples are the quadrats. The stream is a **block**.
:::
:::
:::::

## Three Analyses of the Same 135 Samples {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r lmm-stream-02}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
w_naive <- lm(log_insects ~ reach, data = w_df)
w_fixed <- lm(log_insects ~ reach * stream, data = w_df)
w_mixed <- lmer(
  log_insects ~ reach + (1 | stream) + (1 | stream:reach),
  data = w_df,
  control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))
```

```{r lmm-stream-03}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
w_a1 <- anova(w_naive)
w_a2 <- anova(w_fixed)
w_a3 <- anova(w_mixed)

data.frame(
  model   = c("reach only", "reach * stream, fixed", "mixed"),
  F_value = round(c(w_a1["reach", "F value"], w_a2["reach", "F value"],
                    w_a3["reach", "F value"]), 2),
  den_df  = round(c(w_a1["Residuals", "Df"], w_a2["Residuals", "Df"],
                    w_a3["reach", "DenDF"])),
  p       = format.pval(c(w_a1["reach", "Pr(>F)"], w_a2["reach", "Pr(>F)"],
                          w_a3["reach", "Pr(>F)"]), digits = 1, eps = 0.0001))
```

**The effect was real.** We built in a 30% drop and got *p* = 0.10.
Three streams is three replicates; more samples per reach would not
have helped.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**4 denominator df, not 132**

`(1 | stream:reach)` gives each of the 9 reaches its own offset — it is
the urchin `(1 | patch)`. `(1 | stream)` is the block.

Reach is then tested against how much the willow effect **changes from
stream to stream**: (3 − 1) × (3 − 1) = 4 df.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ All-fixed is the worst of the three**

`reach * stream` looks careful, and gives the biggest *F*. It tests
reach against sample noise, so it only speaks about **these 9 reaches**.
:::
:::
:::::

## Stream: Fixed Block or Random Block? {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r lmm-stream-04}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
# stream as a FIXED block, reach-in-stream still random
w_block <- lmer(
  log_insects ~ reach + stream + (1 | stream:reach),
  data = w_df)

# the 1960s way: collapse to the 9 reach means
w_rcb <- lm(log_insects ~ reach + stream, data = w_means)
```

```{r lmm-stream-05}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
w_a4 <- anova(w_block)
w_a5 <- anova(w_rcb)

data.frame(
  model   = c("stream random", "stream fixed block", "9 reach means"),
  F_value = round(c(w_a3["reach", "F value"], w_a4["reach", "F value"],
                    w_a5["reach", "F value"]), 2),
  den_df  = round(c(w_a3["reach", "DenDF"], w_a4["reach", "DenDF"],
                    w_a5["Residuals", "Df"])),
  p       = round(c(w_a3["reach", "Pr(>F)"], w_a4["reach", "Pr(>F)"],
                    w_a5["reach", "Pr(>F)"]), 3))
```

Identical. For the **reach** test on a balanced design it does not
matter whether the block is fixed or random.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**What is not optional is `(1 | stream:reach)`**

Drop it and the 15 samples become replicates again. Whatever you call
the stream, the **reach** must be in the model as a random term — or
you analyse the 9 reach means.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Which to report with 3 streams**

Same answer as the crayfish: **stream as a fixed block**. Three streams
cannot pin down a variance — `confint()` puts σ~stream~ between 0.08
and 0.88 — and a random block often comes back as exactly 0 with a
*singular fit* warning.

With 6 or more streams, make it random and report the variance.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 8 — The Short Version

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
1. **Repeated measures on an animal** are subsamples of that animal.
   Put the animal in the random part, and put **time on the left of the
   bar** if animals can differ in their rate of change.
2. A random **intercept alone** can make things worse: it shrinks the
   noise but still treats every measurement as a replicate of the slope.
3. **Blocked treatments with subsamples** need the experimental unit as
   a random term — `(1 | stream:reach)` — whatever you do with the
   block.
4. Fixed block and random block give the **same treatment test** on a
   balanced design. With fewer than about 5 blocks, fit the block as
   **fixed**.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 In one sentence**

Before fitting anything, ask **what the treatment was applied to** and
count those. That number, not the number of rows, sets the denominator
df — and `lmer()` will get it right only if that unit is in the model.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Counts, not logs**

Insect counts really want a Poisson or negative binomial response:
`glmer.nb(insects ~ reach + stream + (1 | stream:reach))`. Same random
part; last week's distribution.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 9 · Wrap-Up {.divider}

## Anatomy of a Random Term

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```
y  ~  x  +  (  1 + x   |   lake  )
               -----       ----
               WHAT        ACROSS WHICH
               varies      groups
```

Read the bar as **"is allowed to differ among"**. The left side is
ordinary formula language:

- **`1`** is the **intercept** → each lake gets its own baseline:
  a **random intercept**
- **a variable name** is that variable's **slope** → each lake gets
  its own steepness: a **random slope**
- **`1 + x`** is both, plus the correlation between them

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Say it aloud**

`(1 | lake)` — "the intercept differs among lakes."

`(1 + x | lake)` — "the intercept **and the slope of x** differ among
lakes."
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
In `y ~ x + (1 + x | lake)` the **x appears twice**, doing two jobs:

::: {.compact-table}
| Where | Estimates | Shows up in |
|-------------|---------------------|------------------|
| `y ~ x` | the **average** slope over all lakes | Fixed effects: an estimate and SE |
| `(... x | lake)` | **how much** lakes' slopes differ from it | Random effects: an SD and a Corr |
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Shorthand that catches people**

- `(x | lake)` **is** `(1 + x | lake)` — the intercept is automatic,
  as in `y ~ x`. Write the `1 +` anyway.
- `(0 + x | lake)` is a slope with **no** random intercept.
- The right side must be a **grouping factor**, never a number.
- A predictor can go on the left only if it **varies within** the
  groups. Urchin density does not vary within a patch, so
  `(1 + treat | patch)` cannot be fitted.
:::
:::
:::::

## The `lmer` Formula Cheat-Sheet

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
Read every random term as **`( what varies | across what )`**.

::: {.compact-table}
| Formula | Meaning | Picture |
|------------------|---------------------------|----------------|
| `y ~ x + (1|g)` | random **intercept** per group | parallel lines |
| `y ~ x + (1 + x|g)` | random intercept **and slope** | lines fan or cross |
| `y ~ x + (1 + x||g)` | the same, intercept and slope uncorrelated | lines fan or cross |
| `y ~ x + (0 + x|g)` | random slope only, shared intercept | lines pivot on one point |
| `y ~ x + (1|a) + (1|b)` | two **crossed** random factors | every a meets every b |
| `y ~ x + (1|a/b)` | b **nested** in a — shorthand for `(1|a) + (1|a:b)` | b lives inside one a |
:::

Random slopes were Parts 7 and 8; time-series error structures and the full
set of random-slope spellings get their own reference page:
[Mixed Model Structures](../../vignettes/16_mixed_model_structures_vignette/mixed_model_structures.qmd).

::: callout-important
**⚠️ The confusion to avoid**

`(1|patch)` and `(1|treat:patch)` are **both random-intercept** models.
The `1` is the intercept; what differs is only the **grouping**.
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-tip
**🖐 Do I need `a/b` here?**

Only if the inner IDs **restart** inside each outer level (patch 1,2,3,4
in *every* treatment). Then R cannot tell nesting from crossing and you
must write `(1|treat/patch)`.

Our patches are numbered 1–16 across the whole study, so `(1|patch)`
already says it.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ "boundary (singular) fit"**

A variance was estimated as **exactly 0** — the likelihood hit the edge
of what a variance is allowed to be. It is the REML version of the
moment estimator going negative (Part 4).

Simplify the random effects; do not ignore it.
:::
::::
:::::::

## Wrap-up

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
Today you:

- Decided **fixed vs random** by asking whether you care about *these*
  levels or about *how much they vary*
- Learned a random factor costs **one parameter**, and that
  `(1|group)` is **not** a random slope
- Chose between the ***F*-test (*p* = 0.091)** and the **Wald χ²
  (*p* = 0.043)** — and learned why the *F*-test is right at 16 groups
- Saw **where the variance components come from**: a search over a
  restricted likelihood, not a partition of sums of squares
- Got **ICC = 0.50**, and saw **partial pooling** shrink each patch
  estimate toward its treatment mean
- Fitted the crayfish `lake` **fixed and random**, read `summary()`
  line by line, and saw a random **slope** turn the interaction into a
  variance — and the `range` test from 80 df to **2**
- Gave each chick its **own growth line**, and tested a stream
  treatment against **3 streams**, not 135 samples
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-important
**✅ The one idea to keep**

A mixed model does not "remove" the patch effect — it **estimates** it,
and tests the treatment against the right amount of noise.

The old way *partitioned* variation that was already computed. The new
way *proposes* variances and keeps the ones that make the data most
likely. On a balanced design they agree exactly; everywhere else only
the second still works.
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 Up next**

`glmer()` — a non-normal response **and** a random effect. You now have
both halves.
:::
::::
:::::::

## Before Next Class

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
Take the pine needle data, **collapsed to one value per team per side**
(the two-stage summary from Week 3):

``` r
p_df <- pine_df |>
  group_by(team, side) |>
  summarise(needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm),
            .groups = "drop")

anova(lmer(needle_length_mm ~ side + (1|team), data = p_df))
```

Compare *F* to the **square of** the paired-*t* statistic from Week 4
(*t* = −2.72). You should get ***F* = 7.41, df 1 and 3, *p* = 0.072** —
the paired *t*-test **is** this mixed model.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-tip
**🚀 If you finish early**

Run the same formula on the **raw 64 needles**. You get *p* = 0.057 on
**59** denominator df, not 3 — because `(1|team)` alone assumes `side`
behaves identically in every team, so all 64 needles count as
replicates of the side effect.

Now let each team have its own side difference, by adding
**`+ (1|team:side)`**. R warns **"boundary (singular) fit"**:
σ²~team:side~ comes back as exactly **0**, the df stay at 59, and
nothing is fixed. Four teams cannot separate that variance from zero —
which is why the collapsed 8-value analysis is the defensible one.
:::
:::
:::::

## Readings

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Gotelli & Ellison**, Ch. 10 — The Analysis of Variance, for the random-effects and variance-component material this lecture rebuilds.
- Hurlbert, S. H. (1984). Pseudoreplication and the design of ecological field experiments. *Ecological Monographs, 54*(2), 187–211. The Part 1 reference.
- **Quinn & Keough** (2002), *Experimental Design and Data Analysis for Biologists*, Ch. 9 §9.1 — nested designs and expected mean squares. This is the source of today's worked example.
- Zuur, A. F., et al. (2009). *Mixed Effects Models and Extensions in Ecology with R*. Springer. Ch. 5 is the standard ecological treatment of REML.
- Bates, D., Mächler, M., Bolker, B., & Walker, S. (2015). Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4. *Journal of Statistical Software*, 67(1), 1–48.
::::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 On the dataset**

The sea urchin grazing data are Andrew & Underwood's, as analysed in
Quinn & Keough Ch. 9. The Part 7 crayfish are Sargent & Lodge (2014),
*Evolutionary Applications* 7: 949–961 — the factorial weeks' file.
`ChickWeight` ships with R (Crowder & Hand 1990). The willow stream
data are **simulated** for this lecture. Textbook PDFs are on Canvas.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Why no Whitlock & Schluter**

W&S does not cover mixed models or random effects. For this topic,
Gotelli, Quinn & Keough, and Zuur are the references.
